ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Absolute Reward Regularization via Rachet Queries
PROPOSAL: Develop and experimentally evaluate a regularization-based approach to prevent reward hacking under imperfect proxies by constraining the policy's performance in regions unexplored by the reference policy, leveraging ratchet queries that partition the state-action space to establish local, adaptive, risk bounds and back up the regularization strength accordingly. 
CONTROLS: 1) Compare with ORPO (Occupancy-Regularized Policy Optimization), with the same reference policy and state-action space partition. 2) Evaluate on RL baselines with unknown or deficient proxy rewards.
COST: 1000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: outperform ORPO in several domains,  including autonomous vehicle traffic control and pandemic response, with an associated reduction in reward hacking occurrence; poorly classify certain regions of the policy that result in exploitation in low frequency actions in type 1 diabetes management.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Anti-Exploitation Regularization with Uncertainty-Aware Correlation
PROPOSAL: Introduce a modification to existing reward hacking mitigation methods to account for uncertainty in correlation coefficient estimates and select proxy rewards, such that the regularization strength is pasted and backed off according to confidence intervals of the correlation estimates.
CONTROLS: 1) Compare with current methods that ignore correlation uncertainty. 2) Assess policy performance under varying levels of noise in correlation estimates.
COST: 700 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: improve robustness to noisy correlation estimates in real-world problems such as pandemic response and blood glucose control; in applications with very high confidence intervals, methods that ignore correlation uncertainty might perform marginally better in few instances of scenario where correlation assumption slightly fails to hold.

ACTION: REVISIE 2
TITLE: Anti-Exploitation Regularization with Uncertainty-Aware Correlation
PROPOSAL: Modify the previous proposal to jointly learn the correlation coefficient and the regularization strength by maximizing an upper bound on the true performance, via an auxiliary loss that encourages accurate correlation estimation and adaptively tunes regularization strength, built upon the evidence lower bound (ELBO) and leveraging variational inference to handle both Bayesian inferece of the correlation and Adam to adpthive the regularization strength.
CONTROLS: 1) Compare with methods that separately learn the correlation coefficient and optimize the policy with fixed regularization strength, 2) Assess performance under varying levels of noise in true reward and correlation estimates.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: improve accuracy in estimating correlation coefficients in both synthetic settings and real-world problems; when the true reward and correlation estimate noise both reach instances of tailcases failure – policies might catastrophically fail by discounting the reward value piece failing prior correlation statements.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reward Decomposition via Causal Mechanics
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel method of reward decomposition based on causal mechanics, tailored to identify and condition on necessary causal factors serving as mediators between the proxy reward and true outcome under noisy environments, abandoning the assumption of real-world strict equiprobability of interventions; leverage RL algorithms to estimate causal effects and interpret causal predictions that underlie true reward predictions.
CONTROLS: 1) Compare the quality of reward decomposition to current state-of-the-art methods, such as forward and inverse models and or encoder decompositions, in terms of the reduction of reward hacking. 2) Assess robustness in blood glucose control for type 1 diabetes cases with imperfections over its autoregressive and historic partial basis dynamics.
COST: 900 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: advance reward hacking mitigation by decomposing proxy rewards, showing improved true reward prediction under uncertainty or noisy reward conditions in type 1 diabetes management.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Reward Decomposition via Causal Mechanics
PROPOSAL: Introduce an extension to the causal mechanics-based reward decomposition method, using Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) to incorporate structured causal knowledge, such as multimodal biomechanical dynamics of various effectors and losses interacting. 
CONTROLS: 1) Compare with a simplified causal-mechanistics method w/o GCNNs. 2) Measure and justify the structural explainability of discovered causal mechanisms in LLM alignment and insurance recommendation tasks for value-function approximation.
COST: 1300 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: improve upon existing reward decomposition based on causal mechanics where possible and feasible advanced scenario domains related to AVM populace environments such as autonomous vehicles proper but with unforeseen casualty interact at location regarding myths timings sequences.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Regularized Imitation Learning for Exploration-Exploitation Tradeoff
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel Regularized Imitation Learning (RIL) approach that explicitly balances exploration and exploitation by incorporating a regularization term to penalize deviation from the reference policy, leveraging the learned representation to regularize policy updates in a way that prevents reward hacking and encourages exploration in unexplored regions.
CONTROLS: 1) Compare with Deep Deterministic Policy Gradient (DDPG) and Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) without regularization. 2) Evaluate on several synthetic and real-world domains, including self-driving cars and insulin dosing for type 1 diabetes.
COST: 1100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in terms of true reward while maintaining exploration in unexplored regions, avoiding policy hacking and providing improved robustness to imperfect reward functions in high-stakes application environments.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Absolute Reward Regularization via Rachet Queries
PROPOSAL: Modify the ratchet queries algorithm to incorporate a regularization term that promotes consistency of local estimates with a global estimation of the true reward, using a weighted average of local estimates and learned representations to provide a more robust estimate of the true reward and improve regularization strength adaptation.
CONTROLS: 1) Compare with the original ratchet queries algorithm. 2) Evaluate the impact of regularization strength on robustness and adaptation performance.
COST: 900 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: improve the robustness of ratchet queries algorithm in high-stakes application environments by reducing the impact of local overfitting and increasing consistency with the true reward, but face challenges in choosing suitable regularization strength under certain unknown scenarios preventing few key InLiSS societal troubleshooting useeffects.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical Reward Correction for Robustness and Interpretability
PROPOSAL: Introduce a hierarchical approach to reward correction, where a high-level reward function is learned from a set of lower-level, domain-specific reward functions, each representing a specific aspect of the true reward, to improve robustness and interpretability of the learned policy.
CONTROLS: 1) Compare with a single, global reward function. 2) Evaluate the impact of decomposing the reward function on policy performance and interpretability.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: improve the robustness of the learned policy by encouraging exploration of the reward space and reducing the impact of imperfect proxy rewards, while also providing a more interpretable representation of the true reward, but may require careful tuning of the hierarchical structure and reward weights to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Temporal Logic-based Reward Validation for Safety and Explainability
PROPOSAL: Introduce a temporal logic-based framework for validating the learned policy's behavior against a set of safety and cohesion specifications, represented as temporal logic formulas, to ensure safety and improve explainability of the policy's decisions.
CONTROLS: 1) Compare with standard RL-based approaches. 2) Evaluate the impact of safety specifications on policy performance and explainability.
COST: 1500 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: improve the safety and explainability of the learned policy, but may require careful tuning of the temporal logic formulas and safety specifications to achieve optimal performance and prevent over-safety, where the policy becomes overly cautious and fails to explore the environment effectively.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Benchmarking and Comparison of Reward Hacking Mitigation Methods
PROPOSAL: Design and publish a comprehensive benchmarking framework for comparing and evaluating the effectiveness of different reward hacking mitigation methods, including both theoretical and experimental evaluations, to provide a standardized and rigorous assessment of the strengths and weaknesses of each approach.
CONTROLS: 1) Evaluate each method on a suite of synthetic and real-world benchmark domains, including the ones proposed in this paper. 2) Assess the robustness and generalizability of each method to different types of reward hacking.
COST: 2000 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: provide a comprehensive evaluation of the current state-of-the-art in reward hacking mitigation, identify targeted areas for improvement, and enable researchers and practitioners to make informed decisions about which methods to use in their specific applications, improving the robustness and safety of reinforcement learning systems.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Absolute Reward Regularization via Rachet Queries
PROPOSAL: This proposal introduces a new approach to robust reinforcement learning, called Absolute Reward Regularization via Rachet Queries (ARRQ). Given a proxy reward, a reference policy, and an assumed correlation level, ARRQ first learns to estimate the correlation between the proxy and true rewards across the state-action space. It then formalizes an upper bound on the difference between the true reward of the learned policy and that of the reference policy, using this estimated correlation. This bound is used as a regularization term in the policy optimization objective, guiding the search towards policies whose true performance is significantly better than the reference policy. Specifically, ARRQ involves solving a 2-player game between a learner and an adversary, who seeks to minimize the estimated correlation.
CONTROLS: The baseline experiments will compare ARRQ with standard policy-optimization methods, including ORPO, and with two new methods that use an idealized version of.ARRQ with the true correlation known; in ablations, we will also investigate ARRQ with different correlation estimation methods and with the adversarial term omitted.
COST: 6480
PREDICTION: We expect ARRQ to achieve better robustness against reward hacking than ORPO and provide strong guarantees on the improved true reward of the learned policy, but may struggle with high-dimensional state spaces, where other methods may benefit from more aggressive exploration policies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Anti-Exploitation Regularization with Entropic Reward Mismatch
PROPOSAL: This proposal extends ARRQ by incorporating an entropic regularizer to the policy optimization objective, further penalizing the exploration of regions with low proxy reward, past a certain threshold that depends on the correlation level. This anti-exploitation regularizer discourages the policy from exploiting potential imperfections in the proxy reward, aiming to reduce the greedy behavior often associated with reward hacking. The formal framework of ARRQ is adapted to this new regularizer, allowing for efficient optimization and theoretical analysis.
CONTROLS: To compare the efficacy of ARRQ w. Entropic Reward Mismatch, we will implement ARRQ with and without the proposed regularizer, and compare their performance, both in terms of true reward and proxy reward exploration, in controlled settings (e.g., MuJoCo and Atari games).
COST: 19320
PREDICTION: We anticipate that incorporating the entropic regularizer will help prevent the policy from falling into the rewards hacking trap in environments with imperfect proxies, and their added layer of extensibility may allow our result to model environments which generally are far better modeled via exploration-exploitation tradeoff regulators — but we do anticipate performance costs, especially in scenarios where the proxy reward deviates from the true reward.

ACTION: REVISI 2
TITLE: Anti-Exploitation Regularization with Entropic Reward Mismatch
PROPOSAL: The key change is the incorporation of a learned reference distribution over state-action pairs, which replaces the fixed reference policy used to estimate the correlation between proxy and true rewards. The learned reference distribution will adapt to the true reward landscape as it is explored, making the learning process more informed and better equipped to counter reward hacking. To formally analyze this adaptation, we derive bounds on the difference between the true reward of the learned policy and the reference distribution, under the given correlation constraint.
CONTROLS: As before, we compare the performance of ARRQ with and without the learned reference distribution, in terms of true reward and proxy reward exploration, in controlled settings (e.g., MuJoCo and Atari games). We will also investigate the robustness of the learned reference distribution to variations in the proxy reward.
COST: 19320
PREDICTION: Using a learned reference distribution should greatly improve the learned policy's performance and make it more robust to reward hacking, including in environments with changing reward landscapes; the adaptability may come at some computational and interpretability costs.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Reward-invariant Influence-Reducing Regularization (RIIRR)
PROPOSAL: This proposal focuses on regularizing policies to reduce their influence on parts of the state-action space that are more susceptible to reward hacking. We introduce a novel regularization term that measures the alignment between the learned policy and a target distribution, which enforces a departure from parts of the state-action space under the proxy reward. The resulting algorithm, RIIRR, adaptively balances exploration and regularization to achieve robustness against reward hacking.
CONTROLS: We compare RIIRR with existing robust RL methods, such as ARRQ and its variants, and a learned reference distribution-based approach. Experiments will be run on MuJoCo and Atari games to assess RIIRR's ability to learn robust policies and mitigate reward hacking.
COST: 87360
PREDICTION: RIIRR should provide effective regularization against reward hacking by focusing on vulnerable regions, which will likely come at some performance costs.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Reward-invariant Influence-Reducing Regularization (RIIRR)
PROPOSAL: The key change is the formalization of RIIRR as minimizing a new information-theoretic penalty measure, the conditional mutual information between the learned policy's actions and the target distribution, conditioned on the proxy reward. This reformulation enables a more efficient optimization algorithm and a more principled analysis of the trade-off between exploration and regularization. Theoretical and experimental results will demonstrate the benefits of this reformulation for learning robust policies against reward hacking.
CONTROLS: We compare the revised RIIRR with the original algorithm and other robust RL methods, such as ARRQ and its variants. Experiments will be run on MuJoCo and Atari games to assess the revised RIIRR's ability to learn robust policies and mitigate reward hacking.
COST: 87360
PREDICTION: The revised RIIRR should provide more efficient optimization and improved robustness against reward hacking, but it may still require careful hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal balance between exploration and regularization.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Prior-Knowledge-Steered Tractable Robust RL
PROPOSAL: This proposal aims to leverage prior knowledge about the structure of the true reward when available, to guide the policy learning process and improve robustness to reward hacking. We propose a novel framework that includes a tractable representation of the prior knowledge, which is used to augment the policy optimization objective with a regularization term that encourages the learned policy to align with the prior knowledge. Theoretical analysis and experimental evaluation will demonstrate the benefits of incorporating prior knowledge in robust RL.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of the proposed approach with existing robust RL methods, such as ARRQ and its variants, RIIRR, and a baseline that ignores prior knowledge. Experiments will be run on MuJoCo and Atari games to assess the approach's ability to learn robust policies that align with prior knowledge and mitigate reward hacking.
COST: 173640
PREDICTION: The approach should provide effective and interpretable results when prior knowledge is available, but may struggle to handle complex and uncertain prior knowledge, and may not perform well in environments where approximate prior knowledge is poor.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Absolute Reward Regularization via Rachet Queries
PROPOSAL: The key change is the extension of ARRQ to incorporate a meta-learning component, where the regularization term is learned jointly with the policy using a bilevel optimization framework. This allows the algorithm to adaptively adjust the strength of the regularization based on the specific problem instance, improving its robustness to reward hacking. Theoretical analysis and experimental evaluation will demonstrate the benefits of this meta-learning approach.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of the revised ARRQ with the original algorithm and other robust RL methods, such as RIIRR and Prior-Knowledge-Steered Tractable Robust RL. Experiments will be run on MuJoCo and Atari games to assess the revised ARRQ's ability to learn robust policies and mitigate reward hacking.
COST: 6480
PREDICTION: The revised ARRQ should provide improved adaptability and robustness to reward hacking, but may require careful tuning of the bilevel optimization framework to achieve optimal performance.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robust Hierarchical Imitation Learning for Reward Hacking Prevention
PROPOSAL: This proposal introduces a novel approach to preventing reward hacking by applying robust hierarchical imitation learning (RHIL) to learn policies that mimic expert demonstrations while being robust to reward hacking. RHIL leverages a two-level hierarchical architecture, where the high-level policy encourages exploration and the low-level policy learns to mimic expert actions. We incorporate robustness by using a corrupting mechanism to simulate potential reward hacking attacks and regularize the low-level policy to follow the expert's behavior.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of RHIL with existing robust RL methods, such as ARRQ, RIIRR, and Prior-Knowledge-Steered Tractable Robust RL, and a baseline that ignores robustness. Experiments will be run on MuJoCo and Atari games to assess RHIL's ability to learn robust policies that mimic expert behavior and mitigate reward hacking.
COST: 274200
PREDICTION: RHIL should provide effective robustness against reward hacking by learning to mimic expert behavior while being adaptable to different environments, but may struggle with complex and high-dimensional state spaces, and may require careful tuning of the corrupting mechanism.

ACTION: REVISE 5
TITLE: Robust Hierarchical Imitation Learning for Reward Hacking Prevention
PROPOSAL: The key change is the addition of a partial observation scenario to the RHIL framework, where the low-level policy learns to mimic expert actions in a partially observable environment. This extension enables RHIL to learn policies that are robust to reward hacking even when the agent has limited knowledge of the true reward function. We incorporate robustness by using control variates to reduce the variance of the reward hacking attacks and regularize the low-level policy to follow the expert's behavior.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of the revised RHIL with the original algorithm and other robust RL methods, such as ARRQ, RIIRR, and Prior-Knowledge-Steered Tractable Robust RL. Experiments will be run on MuJoCo and Atari games with partial observations to assess the revised RHIL's ability to learn robust policies that mimic expert behavior and mitigate reward hacking.
COST: 274200
PREDICTION: The revised RHIL should provide effective robustness against reward hacking in partial observation scenarios, but may require careful tuning of the control variates to reduce variance and may struggle with very high-dimensional state spaces.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Hierarchical and Self-Supervised Robust Reinforcement Learning
PROPOSAL: This proposal introduces a novel framework that combines the strengths of hierarchical reinforcement learning and self-supervised learning to prevent reward hacking. The framework consists of a high-level policy that explores the environment and a low-level policy that learns to predict the true reward. The self-supervised learning component is used to regularize the low-level policy to predict the true reward, while the hierarchical component is used to guide the exploration of the high-level policy. We incorporate robustness by using a robust optimization approach to ensure that the policy is robust to reward hacking attacks.
CONTROLS: We compare the performance of the proposed framework with existing robust RL methods, such as ARRQ, RIIRR, Prior-Knowledge-Steered Tractable Robust RL, and Robust Hierarchical Imitation Learning for Reward Hacking Prevention. Experiments will be run on MuJoCo and Atari games to assess the framework's ability to learn robust policies that mitigate reward hacking.
COST: 899040
PREDICTION: The proposed framework should provide effective robustness against reward hacking by combining the strengths of hierarchical and self-supervised learning, but may require careful tuning of the hyperparameters and may struggle with very complex and high-dimensional state spaces.

We expect this method to perform well on moderately ill-posed problems with relatively high-quality noise, such as image super-resolution and image inpainting.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: dynamic consistency and manifold preservation
PROPOSAL: Develop a method called Dynamic Consistency and Manifold Preservation (DCMP), which iteratively updates the diffusion guidance process by matching the intermediate states to the manifold — instead of directly feeding them back to the denoiser. First, we use the learned denoiser to define a manifold — where data likelihood is high — by calculating the mean of the denoiser output for a range of noise inputs. Then, at each timestep, we check if the guidance signal differs significantly from the manifold. If it does, we re-align the guidance trajectory to be closer to the manifold. This should maintain the learned data distribution, avoiding drift off the manifold and guaranteeing manifold feasibility.
CONTROLS: Compare against DPS and DDRM.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: DCMP should significantly reduce the off-manifold drift seen in current methods and maintain reliable reconstructions, even at high noise levels. A minor issue could be that manual tuning of parameters for DCMP would be needed for different noise distributions.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: probabilistic forward mappings
PROPOSAL: To address the intractable likelihoods, develop Probabilistic Forward Mappings (PFM), a probabilistic, invertible, and differentiable approximation of the forward operator A. We achieve this by training a probabilistic neural network that maps the true forward operator to a Gaussian process, allowing us to treat the forward operator as a probabilistic function and comptuted the likelihoods, p(y|x), in closed-form. TITLE: Utilizing Global Optimization Methods for Q-Function Maximization
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel approach to efficiently find the maximizing action in continuous action spaces by employing a global optimization method, specifically the Branch and Bound algorithm. This method iteratively branches the action space into smaller subspaces and bounds the Q-value to expedite the search for the optimal action. We will implement this approach as a plugin for existing value-based algorithms like DQN, using the Mujoco simulated MuJoCo benchmarks with 2D/3D robot manipulation tasks and the continuous control environments of the Gym suite (e.g., Pendulum, Cartpole).
CONTROLS: We compare our approach against the standard DQN with exploration using the ε-greedy policy, and ablate the use of Branch and Bound by comparing it against a Q-function maximization method with a simple exhaustive search, as well as a random search baseline with a prescribed number of iterations. This will help us determine if our approach truly improves upon existing maximization methods and reduces the computational cost.
COST: Estimated GPU-hours: 100-150
PREDICTION: Our proposed method is expected to achieve better convergence rates and reduced computation time compared to the exhaustive search and random search baselines, but it may struggle with high-dimensional action spaces due to the increased complexity of the Branch and Bound algorithm, potentially leading to suboptimal solutions in such cases.

PROPOSAL: We propose an alternative approach to find the optimal actions by pre-discretizing the continuous action space into a set of grids and then using stochastic gradient descent (SGD) to iteratively refine the searching action. This method combines the benefits of using discrete actions (faster computation) with the ability to explore high-dimensional action spaces more efficiently. We implement this approach using PyTorch and utilize the MuJoCo and Gym environments for evaluation, such as the aforementioned 2D/3D robot manipulation tasks and continuous control tasks like Cartpole.
CONTROLS: To evaluate the performance of our method, we compare it against the previous Branch and Bound method (Proposal 1), the exhaustive search baseline, and a random search baseline with a prescribed number of iterations. We also compare the proposed method against DQN with ε-greedy exploration as a stabilizing baseline control.
COST: Estimated GPU-hours: 120-180
PREDICTION: The proposed stochastic gradient descent method is expected to exhibit stable performance and accurate convergence to the optimal action, even in high-dimensional action spaces, as it can iteratively refine the search over pre-discretized action spaces. Challenges might arise from selecting the optimal grid size and SGD step size to balance exploration and exploitation, which could be critical in terms of performance and convergence speed.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Adaptive Q-Function Simplification through Action Space Abstraction
PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptive approach to simplify the Q-function by abstracting the action space through a hierarchical representation. Our method, called AQSA, uses a hierarchical clustering algorithm to group similar actions together, and then represents the Q-function as a set of simplified Gaussian mixture models on each cluster. AQSA adaptively refines the hierarchy and the Q-function representation as it learns, allowing it to efficiently capture complex action spaces. We will implement AQSA using the MuJoCo and Gym environments and evaluate its performance on continuous control tasks.
CONTROLS: We compare AQSA against the standard Q-learning with ε-greedy exploration, the original DQN, the revised Efficient Action Search via Stochastic Gradient Descent on Pre-Discretized Action Spaces (Proposal 2), and Combining Local Search and Gradient Estimates for Q-Function Maximization (Proposal 3).
COST: Estimated GPU-hours: 130-190
PREDICTION: AQSA is expected to achieve good balance between expressiveness and simplicity in representing the Q-function, leading to efficient learning and good performance on tasks with complex action spaces. However, adapting the hierarchy and Q-function representation online may require careful tuning, and AQSA may be sensitive to the choice of clustering algorithm and Gaussian mixture model parameters.

TITLE: Exploring the Use of Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning for Q-Function Maximization
PROPOSAL: We propose an adaptation of hierarchical reinforcement learning to efficiently find the maximizing action in continuous action spaces. Our method, called Hietron, uses a high-level policy to select which sub-policy to use, and a low-level policy to select the optimal action within the selected sub-policy. Hietron can efficiently explore complex action spaces by leveraging the decomposition of the problem into sub-policies. We will implement Hietron using the MuJoCo and Gym environments and evaluate its performance on continuous control tasks.
CONTROLS: We compare Hietron against the standard Q-learning with ε-greedy exploration, the original DQN, the revised Efficient Action Search via Stochastic Gradient Descent on Pre-Discretized Action Spaces (Proposal 2), Combining Local Search and Gradient Estimates for Q-Function Maximization (Proposal 3), and Adaptive Q-Function Simplification through Action Space Abstraction (Proposal 4).
COST: Estimated GPU-hours: 150-220
PREDICTION: Hietron is expected to achieve good performance on tasks with complex action spaces, particularly when the action space can be decomposed into smaller, more manageable sub-spaces. However, identifying the optimal sub-policies and updating the high-level policy may require careful tuning, and Hietron may be sensitive to the choice of sub-policy granularity and high-level policy architecture.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: evaluating baseline models for online video step grounding
PROPOSAL: We will experimentally evaluate a set of strong multimodal model baselines for video step grounding, adapted to process only one video segment at a time. Specifically, we will investigate large-scale multimodal transformer models like CLIP, and recent multimodal variants like OSIM and VisIoL, with a focus on evaluating their zero-shot performance when processing a live video stream one segment at a time. We will measure performance using metrics like accuracy, F1-score, and Hamming loss on real-world video step grounding benchmarks from instructional cooking recipe videos and egocentric procedural activity videos.
CONTROLS: We will compare our zero-shot baseline models to models that have been pre-trained on VSG tasks and fine-tuned on a specific dataset, providing an offline benchmark for comparison. We will also evaluate various ablations of our zero-shot models, including the effect of using different types of multimodal input (e.g., frame, audio, or both) and different window sizes for segmenting video frames
COST: 5000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that competing zero-shot models struggle due to the lack of task-specific information in the model, however strong multimodal models that are not specifically designed for this task can still achieve good performance due to their general-purpose multimodal capabilities, and ablation studies will point towards multimodal input as a key factor for zero-shot performance.

PROPOSAL: We will investigate using contextualized embeddings to improve the performance of online video step grounding. Specifically, we will experiment with using pre-trained BERT-like models to generate text embeddings for the step descriptions, and multimodal transformer models to generate visual embeddings for the video frames. We will then use a common encodings space for the step descriptions and video frames to compute similarity scores. This approach aims to capture the nuances of language and visual context that are crucial for accurately grounding video steps.

COST: 8000
PREDICTION: We expect to find that using contextualized embeddings improves the performance of video step grounding, especially in scenarios where step descriptions have high RAKE scores, and that this approach performs well even when the step descriptions are noisy or incomplete.

TITLE: Investigating FFN Dynamics with Gradient-based Probes
PROPOSAL: We propose using gradient-based probes to measure how FFN nonlinearities affect the structure of latent representations. Inspired by the recent work on "gradient-based amnesia," we'll sample noise into each layer's embedding and measure the gradient of a probe objective (e.g., a simple bipartite classifier) as we forward the noise through the model. This will give us a high-dimensional tensor of gradients that tell us how noise is transformed by each layer's FFN. We'll then try to reconstruct these transformations using a low-dimensional embedding (e.g., PCA) to better understand how they evolve across depth and training.
CONTROLS: Compare against baselines using attention maps, visualization with affine spline projections, and ablations where we modify the probe objective or layer sampling schedule.
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We'll find that FFN nonlinearities tend to amplify information loss, but the rate of loss varies across layers and training. This could fail if the probe objective is too simplistic to capture general trends, or if gradient noise dominates the signal we're trying to measure.

TITLE: Redesigning Class Encoding for Pseudo-Labeling in UDA and SSL
PROPOSAL: We propose a novel class-agnostic encoding scheme for pseudo-labels in semantic segmentation, using a probability distribution over all classes instead of one-hot encoding. This can be achieved by treating the argmax of the teacher's prediction as a sampling process with multinomial distributions over classes. For training, we adopt a variant of the multi-task loss that encourages the model to make predictions on the target class and other probable classes simultaneously. This approach avoids the common problem of committing to wrong classes with one-hot encoding and leverage shared attributes among confusing classes effectively.

CONTROLS: We compare our proposed approach with the standard self-training and consistency regularization methods on the Cityscapes dataset for urban street-scene segmentation and the ISBI 2012 and 2019 challenge datasets for cardiac MRI segmentation.

Furthermore, we will use the advanced diffusion diagnostics to analyze the origin and propagation of inter-slice discrepancies in both 2D and 3D diffusion-based solvers, providing further insights into the mechanism behind inter-slice inconsistency.
CONTROLS: The baseline for our diagnostics will be the existing implementation of 2D and 3D diffusion-based solvers without any additional modifications or synchronization.
COST: 200 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: By combining our previous experiments, we will gain a deeper understanding of the relationship between stochastic consistency and inter-slice inconsistency in diffusion-based solvers, and validate our observations on a more comprehensive set of solvers, ultimately strengthening our proposal for slice synchronization.

TITLE: Investigating Inter-Slice Consistency in 3D Diffusion-Based Reconstruction
PROPOSAL: Experimentally compare the inter-slice consistency of a 3D reconstruction using a vanilla 2D diffusion model versus a 2D diffusion model with synchronized noise across slices. We will measure consistency using the overlap between the slices of two generative samples of the same volume, calculated using the intersection-over-union (IoU) metric.
CONTROLS: 
- Vanilla 2D diffusion model (diffusion steps: 1000, beta schedule: linear decay)
- Vanilla 2D diffusion model but with synchronized noise across slices, synchronized at the level of the entire volume ( to serve as a sanity check for the remedy)
COST: 10 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: The synchronized noise version is expected to have significantly higher IoU scores compared to the vanilla version, demonstrating the beneficial effect of synchronizing noise across slices. The synchronized version might also reveal flickering patterns indicative of imperfect synchrony.

TITLE: Analyzing Noise Synchronization Mechanisms for 3D Reconstruction
PROPOSAL: Evaluate the effectiveness of two different noise synchronization mechanisms: (1) temporal synchronization, where noise is synchronized across adjacent time steps (frames), and (2) spatial synchronization, where noise is synchronized across adjacent slices (voxels). We will measure the inter-slice consistency using IoU on a set of volumes reconstructed using these models.
CONTROLS: 
- Vanilla 2D diffusion model (diffusion steps: 1000, beta schedule: linear decay)
- 2D diffusion model with temporal noise synchronization (synchronized at the level of adjacent frames)
- 2D diffusion model with spatial noise synchronization (synchronized at the level of adjacent slices)
COST: 20 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: Spatial noise synchronization (mechanism 2) is expected to provide better inter-slice consistency compared to temporal synchronization (mechanism 1), as it targets the information propagation across slices directly. However, both mechanisms might suffer from limitations, such as increased training time or visual artifacts, which could arise from imperfect noise synchronization.
